questions.problem: Given that $f(x)={({x}^{2}+2x+1)}^{2},$ the slope at the point $(0,1)$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$

First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f={g}^{2},\,g={x}^{2}+2x+1
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=2g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=2x+2.
$$

Multiplying the two together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2g\cdot (2x+2) \\  & =2({x}^{2}+2x+1)(2x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line at the point where $x=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & =[2({x}^{2}+2x+1)(2x+2){]}_{x=0} \\  & =2((0{)}^{2}+2\cdot (0)+1)(2\cdot (0)+2) \\  & =2(1)(2) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

We use chain rule to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$

$$

$$

$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=4{g}^{3},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=3.
$$

Multiplying the two together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =4{g}^{3}\cdot 3 \\  & =12(3x+1{)}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & =[12(3x+1{)}^{3}{]}_{x=-1} \\  & =12(3\cdot (-1)+1{)}^{3} \\  & =12(-2{)}^{3} \\  & =-96.\end{aligned}
$$

We use the chain rule to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$

First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f={g}^{3},\,g=3-2x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=3{g}^{2},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=-2.
$$

Multiplying the two together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =3{g}^{2}\cdot (-2) \\  & =-6(3-2x{)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line at the point where $x=2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & =(-6{(3-2x)}^{2}){|}_{x=2} \\  & =-6{(3-2(2))}^{2} \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the slope of the tangent line at the point $(2,-1)$ is $m=-6.$ Now, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y+1 & =-6\cdot (x-2) \\ y & =-6x+12-1 \\ y & =-6x+11\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+12x}}$ at the point where $x=2$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=3{x}^{2}+12x.$ Then $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}={u}^{-1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x+12.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\cdot (6x+12) \\  & =-\frac{6x+12}{2\sqrt{(3{x}^{2}+12x{)}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={(-\frac{6x+12}{2\sqrt{(3{x}^{2}+12x{)}^{3}}})|}_{x=2} \\  & =-\frac{6(2)+12}{2\sqrt{(3(2{)}^{2}+12(2){)}^{3}}} \\  & =-\frac{24}{2\sqrt{{36}^{3}}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Function Using the Chain Rule and Prime Notation
questions.worked_solution:
Let $g(x)=8x-7$ and $f(g(x))=g(x{)}^{4}.$ 

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =({g}^{4}{)}^{′}=4{g}^{3}, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =(8x-7{)}^{′}=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =4{g}^{3}\cdot (8) \\  & =32(8x-7{)}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Polynomial Raised to a Power Using the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f = g^5, \qquad g = 3x^4+x^3
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g}  = 5g^4,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x} = 12x^3 + 3x^2.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =5{g}^{4}\cdot (12{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}) \\  & =5(3{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}{)}^{4}(12{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $y = \sqrt{1-x^2},$ find $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}.
$$

Here, we've used $u$ instead of $g$ for the intermediate variable. 

Let $u=1-x^2.$ Then $y = \sqrt u = u^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{2}u^{-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt u}
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}  = -2x.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2x}{2\sqrt{u}} \\  & =-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$
